title: The Middle Way
objective: After this level you can explain why the Buddha rejected both luxury and harsh self-denial, and how the Eightfold Path and meditation put the middle way into practice.
summary: The Buddha rejected both luxury and harsh self-denial and taught a middle way: the Eightfold Path of wisdom, ethics and concentration, with meditation at its heart.

cards.headline: Palace or starvation? The Buddha tried both.
cards.body: He grew up in luxury, then spent six years in harsh self-denial. In his first sermon he called both extremes fruitless. What he taught instead became the heart of Buddhist practice.

cards.headline: The middle way
cards.body: In that first sermon, the Buddha described a middle way between two extremes: self-indulgence, and self-mortification, the punishing of your own body. He rejected both as fruitless. He spoke from experience, having lived each one, first as a prince and then as an ascetic. The middle way is not a shrug halfway between. It is a path of its own.

cards.headline: Eight parts, three trainings
cards.body: The middle way has a map: the Eightfold Path. Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness and right concentration. Buddhist tradition groups them into three trainings. Wisdom: view and intention. Ethics: speech, action and livelihood. Concentration: effort, mindfulness and concentration. Notice how everyday some are: how you talk, how you earn a living.

cards.headline: Sitting still on purpose
cards.body: The third training is where meditation lives. Buddhists practice samatha, calming meditation, and vipassana, insight meditation, learning to watch their own thoughts and feelings with detachment. Mindfulness and concentration aren't extras bolted on: they are two of the path's eight parts.

cards.headline: The Middle Way: the takeaways
learned: The middle way avoids both luxury and self-torture
The Eightfold Path groups into wisdom, ethics and concentration

questions.prompt: Which of these is one of the eight parts of the Eightfold Path?

options.label: Right fasting
options.rationale: Harsh fasting was an extreme he rejected.

options.label: Right wealth
options.rationale: Not on the list; right livelihood is.

options.label: Right pilgrimage
options.rationale: Pilgrimage isn't one of the eight.

questions.explanation: The eight: right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration.

questions.prompt: Why did the Buddha reject both a life of luxury and harsh self-denial?

options.label: His teachers ordered him to farm
options.rationale: He rejected both after living them.

options.label: The law banned luxury for princes
options.rationale: It was his own teaching, from experience.

options.label: He thought only monks should fast
options.rationale: He rejected harsh self-denial for everyone.

questions.explanation: In his first sermon he called both self-indulgence and self-mortification fruitless and taught the middle way.

questions.prompt: The Eightfold Path is also one of Level 52's Four Noble Truths. Which one?

options.label: The third: cessation
options.rationale: The third says suffering can end: nirvana.

options.label: The fourth: the path to the end of suffering

questions.explanation: The fourth noble truth is the path to the end of suffering, and that path is the Eightfold Path.
